not_modelled.what: Social Security subtraction under age 55, only for benefits received due to the death of the person originally entitled to them, up to 20,000 a person. A projection cannot tell survivor benefits from other benefits (SSDI is not subtractable under 55).

Pension and annuity subtraction under age 55 for a secondary beneficiary (widow, dependent child) of the person who earned the pension: up to 20,000 less the line 3 Social Security subtraction. A projection cannot tell inherited pension or IRA income from the person's own.

PERA/DPSRS subtraction for Colorado PERA contributions made July 1, 1984 to December 31, 1986, or Denver Public Schools retirement contributions made in 1986. The amount is set in a Department publication that is not in the sources.
Interest on U.S. government bonds, treasury bills and other U.S. obligations is subtracted (DR 0104AD line 2); Fannie Mae and Ginnie Mae interest is not.
Agricultural land capital gain subtraction, up to 100,000, for a farmer (federal Schedule F) who sold agricultural land in Colorado.

approximations.what: Tax is figured on the exact income at 4.4%; below 50,000 the booklet uses the tax table, which taxes each 100-dollar row at its midpoint and rounds to the dollar.
approximations.size: At most about 2 dollars a year (4.4% of half a 100-dollar row, plus rounding).

approximations.what: The standard or itemized federal deduction addback (DR 0104 line 4) is not applied: when federal AGI exceeds 300,000, the federal deduction above 12,000 (single, married filing separately, head of household) or 16,000 (joint) is added back.
approximations.size: 4.4% of the federal deduction above 12,000 or 16,000, only in years federal AGI exceeds 300,000.

approximations.what: The state income tax addback (line 2, Schedule A state income tax) and the qualified business income deduction addback (line 3, AGI over 500,000 or 1,000,000 joint, or a SALT Parity Election) are not applied.
approximations.size: 4.4% of the amount added back; only for itemizers who deduct state income tax, or households with a section 199A deduction.

approximations.what: The pension cap is reduced by each person's taxable Social Security (the record's line 3 or line 5 subtraction). That equals the printed rule whenever the Social Security subtraction is the person's full taxable benefit, and also when it is limited to 20,000 (the 55-64 pension cap is then used up either way). How a joint return's taxable Social Security (Form 1040 line 6b) is split between spouses is left to a Department publication not in the sources; the projection splits it the way the household's facts do.
approximations.size: 4.4% of any difference in the split, at most 4.4% of 24,000 = 1,056 a person a year.

approximations.what: Roth conversions are left out of the pension subtraction's covers (covers_unclear in the record). If Colorado counts a conversion as IRA income on line 4, this overstates tax for a converter aged 55 or older whose other pension and IRA income leaves the cap unused.
approximations.size: At most 4.4% of 24,000 = 1,056 a person a year at 65 or older, 4.4% of 20,000 = 880 at 55-64.

approximations.what: Military retirement pay of a person 55 or older is left out of the pension subtraction (covers_unclear in the record); the booklet's separate 15,000 military subtraction is for people 54 or younger only.
approximations.size: At most 1,056 a person a year at 65 or older and 880 at 55-64, if line 4 does take military retirement.

approximations.what: The 55-64 full Social Security subtraction has thresholds printed only for single (75,000) and married filing jointly (95,000). Read literally, a head of household or married filing separately filer gets only the 20,000-limited subtraction; a consumer that falls back to the single threshold for these statuses allows the full subtraction up to 75,000.
approximations.size: 4.4% of taxable Social Security above 20,000 a person, for a head of household or separate filer aged 55-64 with federal AGI at or under 75,000.

approximations.what: A projection that cannot tell Colorado bonds from other states' bonds treats all tax-exempt interest as other-state and adds it back.
approximations.size: 4.4% of the interest from Colorado bonds issued on or after May 1, 1980.

approximations.what: Interest on U.S. Treasury obligations is taxed (the projection cannot tell it from other interest).
